overview: Git is the tool that tracks the history of your project on your own machine; a remote is a named reference (default name 'origin') to a copy of that same repository hosted somewhere else - usually on a platform like GitHub - so a whole team can share one source of truth.

The three everyday moves are push (upload your local commits to the remote), fetch (download the remote's commits without touching your working files), and pull (fetch and then merge those commits into your branch). Cloning a repo sets 'origin' up automatically.

GitHub is a hosting-and-collaboration platform built on top of Git: it stores the remote, and adds pull requests, code review, issues, forks, protected branches, and CI/CD (GitHub Actions) so data teams can review pipeline code and run tests before it ever reaches the main branch.
learningObjectives: Explain what a remote is, connect a local repo to GitHub with 'git remote add origin', set an upstream with 'git push -u', and inspect remotes with 'git remote -v'.
Push, fetch, and pull confidently - including the difference between fetch (download only) and pull (download plus merge) - and choose HTTPS vs SSH with the right authentication.
Collaborate on GitHub using branches and pull requests, and recover from a rejected non-fast-forward push by pulling (or rebasing) first, resolving, and pushing again.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A remote is a named bookmark stored in a repository's configuration that points to the URL of another copy of the same repository (for example 'origin -> git@github.com:team/pipelines.git'). Git is a distributed version-control system: every clone contains the full history, and remotes are how those clones exchange commits. The core network operations are push (transfer local commits and update the remote branch to point at them), fetch (download new objects and update the remote-tracking branches like origin/main without altering your working tree), and pull (a fetch followed by a merge - or a rebase with --rebase - into your current branch). A tracking (or upstream) branch links a local branch to a remote branch so plain 'git push' and 'git pull' know where to go; you establish it with 'git push -u origin <branch>'. GitHub is a commercial hosting platform that stores remotes and layers collaboration features - pull requests, code review, issues, forks, protected branches, and GitHub Actions CI/CD - on top of the underlying Git protocol.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Imagine your project is a shared document. Git on your laptop is like tracking every edit you make locally, even offline. A remote is the shared copy everyone agrees is the master version, kept on a server - GitHub is the most popular place to keep it, and 'origin' is just the nickname your laptop uses for that shared copy. 'Push' is uploading your latest edits to the shared copy so teammates can see them. 'Fetch' is downloading what others have added so you can look before you touch your own work. 'Pull' is fetch plus 'merge it into what I'm working on right now'. GitHub adds the office around the shared document: a place to leave comments on proposed changes (pull requests), an inbox of tasks (issues), and a robot that automatically checks every change (GitHub Actions) before it's allowed in. Git is the tool; GitHub is the building it lives in.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Git was created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 to manage Linux kernel development after the free license for the previous tool (BitKeeper) was revoked; it was designed from the start to be distributed, fast, and to let thousands of developers exchange changes without a single central server. Because Git is distributed, the concept of a 'remote' is central - there is no privileged master repository built into Git itself, only clones that agree to sync with each other. GitHub launched in 2008 and popularized the idea of a social, web-based home for Git repositories, introducing the pull request as the unit of collaboration and code review; it was acquired by Microsoft in 2018. Rivals like GitLab (2011) and Bitbucket followed with the same model. Over the 2010s, GitHub added issues, forks, and eventually GitHub Actions (2019) for built-in CI/CD. For data engineers this history matters because pipeline code (Airflow DAGs, dbt models, Spark jobs) is now developed exactly like software - versioned in Git, hosted on GitHub, reviewed via pull requests, and deployed automatically when tests pass.

whyItMatters.business: Pipeline code that lives only on one engineer's laptop is a single point of failure and a compliance risk; pushing it to a hosted remote like GitHub gives the business a durable, backed-up, auditable source of truth that survives a lost laptop and lets any team member pick up the work.
whyItMatters.engineering: Collaboration on data pipelines depends on a shared remote: engineers push feature branches, open pull requests so peers can review dbt models or DAG changes, and pull each other's work - fetch and pull are how the team's changes actually reach your machine so you build on current code, not a stale copy.
whyItMatters.scalability: A hosted remote plus pull requests scales a two-person project to a hundred contributors: branch protection, required reviews, and CI checks let many people change the same pipeline repo safely without stepping on each other or breaking main.
whyItMatters.cost: GitHub Actions running tests and linting automatically on every push catches broken SQL or a bad DAG before it ships, avoiding the far larger cost of a corrupted production table or a failed overnight load that pages the on-call engineer.
whyItMatters.reliability: Requiring pull requests, review, and passing CI on a protected main branch means no untested change reaches production; combined with keeping secrets out of the repo, this is what makes a shared pipeline codebase trustworthy enough to deploy automatically.

coreComponents.name: Remote and origin (git remote)
coreComponents.definition: A remote is a named URL pointing to another copy of the repository; 'origin' is the conventional default name Git gives the remote you cloned from. The 'git remote' command lists, adds, and inspects these references.
coreComponents.purpose: To give the local repo a short, memorable handle for the hosted copy so push/fetch/pull know where to send and receive commits without retyping the full URL.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Store the URL(s) for fetch and push, list configured remotes ('git remote -v'), add new ones ('git remote add'), rename or remove them, and let you point a project at GitHub, GitLab, or any Git host.
coreComponents.examples: git remote -v | git remote add origin git@github.com:team/pipelines.git | git remote add upstream https://github.com/org/dbt-project.git | git remote rename origin gh

coreComponents.name: Cloning and tracking branches (git clone, upstream)
coreComponents.definition: Cloning downloads a full copy of a remote repository and automatically configures 'origin'. A tracking (upstream) branch links a local branch to a remote branch so bare 'git push'/'git pull' know the target.
coreComponents.purpose: To get a working copy of a hosted repo in one step and to bind local branches to their remote counterparts so you don't have to specify the remote and branch every time.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Download all history and set up origin ('git clone'), create the local main tracking origin/main, and establish upstreams for new branches with 'git push -u origin <branch>' so future push/pull are just 'git push'.
coreComponents.examples: git clone git@github.com:team/pipelines.git | git push -u origin main | git branch -vv (shows upstreams) | git status (reports ahead/behind of @{upstream})

coreComponents.name: Push, fetch, and pull
coreComponents.definition: Push uploads local commits and moves the remote branch to point at them; fetch downloads new remote commits into remote-tracking branches without merging; pull runs fetch then merges (or rebases) into your current branch.
coreComponents.purpose: To synchronize commits between your machine and the hosted remote - sharing your work (push) and integrating others' work (fetch/pull).
coreComponents.responsibilities: Transfer objects over HTTPS or SSH, update origin/<branch> pointers, merge or rebase remote changes into local branches, and refuse pushes that would overwrite remote history (non-fast-forward) until you integrate first.
coreComponents.examples: git push origin main | git fetch origin | git pull | git pull --rebase | git push -u origin feature/add-orders-model

coreComponents.name: GitHub collaboration layer (PRs, review, forks, Actions)
coreComponents.definition: GitHub is the hosting platform that stores the remote and adds pull requests (proposed merges open for review), code review comments, forks (personal server-side copies), issues, protected branches, and GitHub Actions for CI/CD.
coreComponents.purpose: To turn a shared Git remote into a collaboration workflow where changes are reviewed and automatically tested before merging into the main branch that ships to production.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Host the canonical remote, run CI (tests/lint) on push and PR via Actions, enforce branch protection and required reviews on main, track work in issues, and enable the fork-and-PR open-source model as well as shared-repo team workflows.
coreComponents.examples: gh repo clone team/pipelines | gh pr create --fill | gh pr status | protected 'main' requiring 1 review + green CI before merge

internalWorking: Git stores your project as a chain of commits, each a snapshot pointing to its parent, and a branch is just a movable pointer to the newest commit. A remote is an entry in the repo's .git/config recording a name (origin) and its fetch/push URLs; alongside your local branches Git keeps remote-tracking branches like 'origin/main' that record where the remote's branches were the last time you talked to it.

Cloning contacts the remote, downloads the entire object database (all commits, trees, and blobs), writes them locally, sets 'origin' to the source URL, creates remote-tracking branches for what the server had, and checks out the default branch (usually main) as a local branch that tracks 'origin/main'.

'git fetch' opens a connection to the remote over HTTPS or SSH, asks which commits it has that you lack, downloads only those missing objects, and advances your remote-tracking pointers (origin/main) - it never touches your working files or local branch, which is why fetch is always safe. 'git pull' is exactly a fetch followed by an integration step: by default a merge of origin/main into your current branch, or a rebase if you pass --rebase or configure it.

'git push' is the reverse: it sends the commits the remote lacks and asks it to move its branch pointer to your newest commit. The server only accepts this if the move is a 'fast-forward' - your commit is a direct descendant of what the remote currently points to. If someone else pushed in the meantime, the remote's branch has commits you don't have, the move is not a fast-forward, and the server rejects the push with a 'non-fast-forward' error to avoid silently discarding their work.

Authentication happens per connection: HTTPS URLs (https://github.com/...) require a username and a Personal Access Token (plain account passwords were deprecated by GitHub in 2021), usually cached by a credential helper; SSH URLs (git@github.com:...) use a public/private key pair where your public key is registered on GitHub and your private key stays on your machine. GitHub's 'gh' CLI wraps these operations - cloning, creating pull requests, and managing auth - by calling the GitHub API over HTTPS with a stored token.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Local repo (commits + branches) -> configure remote 'origin' (git remote add / git clone) -> set upstream (git push -u) -> git push uploads local commits (fast-forward only) -> teammate pushes -> git fetch downloads their commits into origin/main -> git pull (fetch + merge/rebase) integrates them locally -> open a Pull Request on GitHub -> code review + GitHub Actions CI -> merge into protected main -> CD deploys the pipeline
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. You have a local Airflow project with a few commits but no remote. You create an empty repository on GitHub, then connect them: 'git remote add origin git@github.com:team/pipelines.git'. This just writes the name-to-URL mapping into .git/config; nothing is uploaded yet.

2. You publish your main branch and bind it to the remote in one step: 'git push -u origin main'. Git uploads all your commits, creates 'main' on the server, and sets your local main to track 'origin/main' so future syncs are just 'git push' and 'git pull'. You confirm the wiring with 'git remote -v' and 'git branch -vv'.

3. To add a feature you branch off: 'git switch -c feature/add-orders-model', make and commit your changes, then publish the branch with 'git push -u origin feature/add-orders-model'. On GitHub you open a Pull Request; GitHub Actions automatically runs your dbt/SQL tests and linting against the proposed change.

4. Meanwhile a teammate merged their own PR into main. When you run 'git fetch origin', Git downloads their commits into 'origin/main' but leaves your files untouched; 'git status' now reports your branch is 'behind'. You integrate with 'git pull --rebase origin main' so your feature commits replay cleanly on top of the latest main.

5. You try to push a follow-up to main directly and it's rejected with a non-fast-forward error because the remote moved. You 'git pull --rebase', resolve any conflicts, run tests locally, push again successfully, and once your PR has a passing CI check and an approving review, it merges into the protected main branch and the deployment pipeline ships it.

keyTerminology.meaning: A named reference in your repo config to a hosted copy of the repository; 'origin' is the default name for the remote you cloned from or first added.
keyTerminology.importance: Every push, fetch, and pull targets a remote; understanding that 'origin' is just a nickname for a URL demystifies where your commits actually go.

keyTerminology.meaning: The link between a local branch and a specific remote branch (its @{upstream}), set with 'git push -u', that lets plain 'git push'/'git pull' know the destination.
keyTerminology.importance: Without an upstream, Git can't tell where to push or pull; setting it turns verbose commands into one-word ones and lets 'git status' report ahead/behind counts.

keyTerminology.meaning: Fetch downloads remote commits into remote-tracking branches without changing your working files; pull is a fetch immediately followed by a merge (or rebase) into your current branch.
keyTerminology.importance: Knowing pull also merges explains why pull can create merge commits or conflicts while fetch never does - fetch lets you inspect before integrating.

keyTerminology.meaning: A push the remote refuses because the remote branch has commits your local branch lacks, so accepting your push would discard them; you must fetch/pull first.
keyTerminology.importance: It's the single most common push failure; recognizing it tells you to pull (or rebase) and try again rather than reaching for a dangerous --force.

keyTerminology.meaning: A GitHub feature that proposes merging one branch into another, opening it for review, discussion, and automated CI checks before the merge happens.
keyTerminology.importance: PRs are the unit of collaboration on GitHub - the place where pipeline changes are reviewed and tested, and are required to reach a protected main branch.

importantConcepts.concept: Git vs GitHub: the tool vs the platform
importantConcepts.explanation: Git and GitHub are constantly confused but are different things. Git is the free, open-source version-control tool that runs on your machine and tracks history entirely locally - you can use Git with no internet and no GitHub account at all. GitHub is a commercial web platform (owned by Microsoft) that hosts Git repositories and wraps them in collaboration features Git itself does not provide: a web UI, pull requests, code review comments, issues, forks, access control, protected branches, and GitHub Actions for CI/CD. Git can talk to many hosts - GitLab, Bitbucket, a plain server, or GitHub - because the 'remote' is just a URL. So 'git push' is a Git operation that uploads commits to whatever remote you configured, while 'opening a pull request' is a GitHub feature layered on top. A useful mental split: Git manages the history; GitHub manages the collaboration around that history.

importantConcepts.concept: Fetch is safe, pull integrates - and why pull can surprise you
importantConcepts.explanation: Both fetch and pull download commits from the remote, but only pull changes your working branch. 'git fetch' updates your remote-tracking branches (like origin/main) and stops there - your files, your current branch, and your commits are untouched, so fetch can never cause a conflict or lose work. This makes fetch the cautious choice: fetch, then run 'git log origin/main' or 'git diff' to see what changed before deciding how to integrate. 'git pull' does the fetch and then immediately merges origin/main into your current branch (or rebases with --rebase). That integration step is where merge commits and merge conflicts appear, and where beginners get surprised - a pull can suddenly stop mid-way asking you to resolve conflicts, or create a messy merge commit. Many teams prefer 'git pull --rebase' to keep history linear. The takeaway: fetch is 'just show me', pull is 'show me and combine it into what I'm doing right now'.

importantConcepts.concept: Why pushes get rejected: non-fast-forward and the correct fix
importantConcepts.explanation: When you push, Git asks the remote to move its branch pointer to your latest commit. The server only allows this if the change is a 'fast-forward' - meaning the remote's current commit is an ancestor of yours, so no existing remote history is lost. If a teammate pushed while you were working, the remote branch now has commits you don't have; moving it to your commit would abandon theirs, so the server rejects the push with 'Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not have locally' (a non-fast-forward error). The correct fix is to integrate the remote's work first: 'git pull --rebase' (or a plain 'git pull') downloads their commits and replays yours on top, after which your push is a clean fast-forward and succeeds. The dangerous shortcut is 'git push --force', which overwrites the remote and can erase a colleague's commits - avoid it on shared branches; prefer '--force-with-lease' only when you fully understand you are rewriting your own branch's history.

importantConcepts.concept: Two collaboration models: shared-repo team flow vs fork-and-PR
importantConcepts.explanation: GitHub supports two common workflows built on the same push/pull mechanics. In the shared-repository model - typical inside a company data team - everyone has write access to one repo; each person creates a feature branch, pushes it to origin, and opens a pull request to merge into a protected main branch after review and passing CI. This is fast and simple because there is one remote ('origin') everyone shares. In the fork-and-pull-request model - typical for open-source and for contributors without write access - you 'fork' the project, which creates your own server-side copy on GitHub; you clone your fork (origin), add the original as a second remote ('upstream'), push branches to your fork, and open a PR from your fork's branch to the original repo. You keep your fork current by pulling from 'upstream'. Both models converge on the same idea: work on a branch, propose it via a PR, get it reviewed and tested, then merge - the only difference is whether you push to the shared repo or to your own fork.

variationsAndTypes: **Remote URL protocols:** HTTPS (https://github.com/org/repo.git - works everywhere, uses username + Personal Access Token), SSH (git@github.com:org/repo.git - uses a key pair, no password prompts once set up), and the gh CLI which uses GitHub's API over HTTPS with a stored token.
**Sync operations:** push (upload commits), fetch (download only, safe), pull (fetch + merge), pull --rebase (fetch + replay your commits on top for linear history).

**Multiple remotes:** origin (your main/hosted copy) and upstream (the original repo you forked from) - common in the open-source fork workflow, kept in sync via 'git fetch upstream' then merge/rebase.

**Collaboration workflows:** shared-repository model (one repo, everyone branches and opens PRs) versus fork-and-pull-request model (fork, push to your copy, PR to the original) used by open-source projects.

**Git hosting platforms:** GitHub (largest, GitHub Actions CI), GitLab (built-in CI/CD, self-hostable), Bitbucket (Atlassian/Jira integration), and self-hosted bare Git servers - all speak the same Git remote protocol.
advantages: **Shared source of truth:** a hosted remote gives the whole team one backed-up, always-available copy of the pipeline code, so work survives a lost laptop and anyone can pick it up.
**Safe collaboration at scale:** branches plus pull requests let many engineers change the same repo without overwriting each other, and required reviews stop unvetted changes reaching main.
**Automated quality gates:** GitHub Actions runs tests and linting on every push and PR, catching broken SQL, DAG errors, or failing dbt tests before they ship.
**Full auditable history everywhere:** because Git is distributed, every clone has the complete history, and the remote records who changed what, when, and why (via PRs and commit messages).
**Offline-first, sync-when-ready:** you commit locally without a network and push only when you choose, so connectivity never blocks your work and pushes are deliberate.
disadvantages: **Not automatic backup of everything:** only the branches you actually push are on the remote; uncommitted work and un-pushed local branches exist solely on your machine and can be lost.
**Merge conflicts and history confusion:** pulls can trigger conflicts, and force-pushes or careless rebases on shared branches can erase teammates' commits if misused.
**Authentication friction:** HTTPS tokens expire and SSH keys must be set up correctly; a common early stumbling block is a push failing on auth rather than on Git itself.

**Platform lock-in and outages:** relying on GitHub-specific features (Actions, PR automation) ties you to the platform, and a GitHub outage can block CI and merges even though Git itself is distributed.
**Secrets leakage risk:** it's easy to accidentally commit and push credentials or config with passwords, and once pushed to a shared remote they must be treated as compromised.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use a hosted remote like GitHub for any project more than one person touches, or any pipeline code that must be reviewed, tested, and deployed - the shared-repo + PR flow for internal teams, the fork + PR flow for open-source or external contributors. Use fetch when you want to inspect before integrating, and pull (often --rebase) for your normal 'get the latest' step.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid pushing large binary data, datasets, or secrets to a code remote - use object storage or a data catalog and keep credentials in a secrets manager. Avoid 'git push --force' on shared branches, and avoid relying on the remote as your only backup for un-pushed work. For a truly private throwaway experiment, a remote may be unnecessary overhead.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Think of Git as the private notebook on your desk where you draft and track every revision, and the remote (origin on GitHub) as the shared master binder in the office library that the whole team treats as official. 'Push' is walking your finished pages over and filing them in the master binder so everyone can read them. 'Fetch' is photocopying whatever new pages others have filed and bringing the copies back to your desk to read - without changing your own drafts. 'Pull' is fetching those copies and then physically merging them into your current draft. A 'pull request' is pinning your proposed pages to the office board with a note 'please review before we file these', where colleagues comment and an automated checker (GitHub Actions) verifies them before a librarian (branch protection) allows them into the master binder. And a rejected push is the librarian saying 'someone filed pages after you last copied the binder - go merge their pages into yours first, then file'.

commonMisconceptions.myth: git push automatically backs up all my branches to GitHub.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Push only uploads the branch (or branches) you explicitly push. Un-pushed local branches, and any uncommitted changes, live only on your machine. To have a branch on the remote you must push it - 'git push -u origin <branch>' - and 'git push' with no arguments pushes only the current branch's upstream, not everything.

commonMisconceptions.myth: GitHub and Git are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Git is the version-control tool that runs locally and works with no internet or account; GitHub is a hosting platform built on Git that adds pull requests, review, issues, and Actions CI/CD. You can use Git without GitHub, and Git can push to other hosts like GitLab or Bitbucket - GitHub is just one very popular place to keep the remote.

commonMisconceptions.myth: git pull and git fetch do the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Fetch only downloads remote commits into your remote-tracking branches and never touches your working files, so it's always safe. Pull does that fetch and then merges (or rebases) the changes into your current branch, which can create merge commits or conflicts. Fetch is 'show me'; pull is 'show me and combine it in'.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Use a hosted remote (GitHub) as the single source of truth, a clear branching strategy (short-lived feature branches, trunk-based or GitFlow), and required pull requests so hundreds of contributors can safely change the same pipeline repo; monorepos or per-service repos are both viable depending on team size.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Protect the main branch with required reviews and required passing CI checks so no untested pipeline change merges; rely on Git's distributed nature (every clone is a full copy) as resilience against remote data loss.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Because every clone holds the entire history, a corrupted or briefly unavailable remote does not lose committed work - developers still have it locally and can re-push; keep at least the main branches always pushed so nothing important lives only on one laptop.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Watch CI status on pushes and PRs (GitHub Actions), track failed pipeline deployments triggered by merges, monitor branch protection compliance, and alert on force-pushes or direct pushes to protected branches.
productionConsiderations.security: Never commit secrets; use a secrets manager and GitHub Actions encrypted secrets, add a .gitignore and secret-scanning, enforce SSH keys or short-lived tokens, require signed commits or 2FA, and restrict who can push to or merge into protected branches.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Catch failures cheaply and early: CI running tests/linting on push prevents costly broken production loads; cache CI dependencies and limit expensive workflows to relevant paths to control GitHub Actions minutes.
productionConsiderations.performance: Keep repos lean (avoid committing large data/binaries - use Git LFS or external storage), use shallow clones in CI ('--depth 1') to speed checkouts, and fetch rather than re-clone to sync large repos efficiently.

codeExamples.title: Connect a local repo to GitHub (git remote add, git push -u) and clone an existing one
codeExamples.overview: Wire up a local project to a new GitHub repository, publish the main branch, verify the remote - and separately, clone a repo that already exists.
codeExamples.code:
# --- Publish an EXISTING local repo to a new empty GitHub repo ---

# 1) Confirm you have commits and see if any remote is set (none yet)
git log --oneline -1
git remote -v          # prints nothing if no remote is configured

# 2) Add the GitHub repo as the remote named 'origin' (SSH URL)
git remote add origin git@github.com:team/pipelines.git
#    HTTPS alternative:
#    git remote add origin https://github.com/team/pipelines.git

# 3) Verify the remote name -> URL mapping
git remote -v

# 4) Push main AND set it as the upstream (-u) so future pushes are just 'git push'
git push -u origin main

# 5) Confirm the local branch now tracks origin/main
git branch -vv

# --- Alternatively, CLONE a repo that already exists on GitHub ---
#     This creates the folder, downloads full history, and sets 'origin' automatically.
git clone git@github.com:team/pipelines.git
cd pipelines
git remote -v          # origin is already configured by clone
codeExamples.breakdown: 'git remote add origin <url>' writes a name-to-URL mapping into .git/config; nothing is uploaded yet. 'git remote -v' lists remotes with their fetch and push URLs so you can confirm the wiring. 'git push -u origin main' uploads all local commits, creates 'main' on the server, and the '-u' sets the upstream so later you can type just 'git push'/'git pull'. 'git branch -vv' shows each local branch and the remote branch it tracks. 'git clone' does all of this in reverse for an existing repo - it downloads everything and configures 'origin' for you automatically.

codeExamples.commonIssues: 'remote origin already exists' means one is set - use 'git remote set-url origin <url>' to change it, or 'git remote remove origin' first. HTTPS pushes now require a Personal Access Token, not your account password (deprecated by GitHub in 2021); SSH pushes fail with 'Permission denied (publickey)' if your SSH key isn't added to GitHub. Pushing to a repo that already has commits online can be rejected as non-fast-forward - see the third example.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Prefer SSH for day-to-day work to avoid repeated token prompts, or use a credential helper ('git config --global credential.helper') to cache HTTPS tokens. Always use '-u' on the first push of a branch so subsequent syncs are one word. Use 'gh repo create' to create the GitHub repo and set the remote in a single step from the terminal.

codeExamples.title: The daily collaboration loop: pull, branch, push, open a PR (with fetch vs pull)
codeExamples.overview: Start from the latest main, create a feature branch, push it, open a pull request with the gh CLI, and see the difference between fetch (inspect) and pull (integrate).
codeExamples.code:
# 1) Get on main and integrate everyone's latest work before starting
git switch main
git pull                       # fetch + merge origin/main into local main

# 2) Create a feature branch for your change
git switch -c feature/add-orders-model

# 3) ...edit dbt models / DAGs... then stage and commit
git add models/orders.sql
git commit -m "Add orders staging model"

# 4) Publish the branch and set its upstream so 'git push' works later
git push -u origin feature/add-orders-model

# 5) Open a pull request from this branch into main (GitHub CLI)
gh pr create --base main --title "Add orders staging model" \
             --body "New dbt staging model for orders; tests included."

# --- FETCH vs PULL: inspect before integrating ---

# fetch only DOWNLOADS remote commits into origin/main; your files are untouched
git fetch origin
git log --oneline main..origin/main   # see what's new on the remote before merging

# pull = fetch + merge (integrates the new commits into your current branch)
git pull
codeExamples.breakdown: 'git switch main' then 'git pull' ensures you branch off the newest code (a fetch plus merge of origin/main). 'git switch -c <name>' creates and moves to a feature branch. After committing, 'git push -u origin <branch>' publishes it and records the upstream. 'gh pr create' opens a GitHub pull request from the terminal, targeting main. The fetch-vs-pull block shows the key distinction: 'git fetch' downloads remote commits into origin/main without changing your working files, and 'git log main..origin/main' lets you preview exactly what's new; 'git pull' does that fetch and then merges those commits into your current branch.

b34f0e2 Fix customers model column type
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting to pull main before branching means you build on stale code and hit conflicts later. 'gh: command not found' means the GitHub CLI isn't installed ('brew install gh') or authenticated ('gh auth login'). Running 'git pull' with local uncommitted changes can abort with 'Your local changes would be overwritten' - commit or stash first. Confusing fetch with pull: after 'git fetch' your files are unchanged; you must still merge/pull to actually integrate.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use 'gh pr create --fill' to auto-populate the title/body from your commits. Prefer 'git pull --rebase' to keep feature history linear before pushing. Use 'git fetch' + 'git log main..origin/main' when you want to review incoming changes before integrating, and set 'git config --global pull.rebase true' if your team standardizes on rebase pulls.

codeExamples.title: Recover from a rejected (non-fast-forward) push with pull --rebase
codeExamples.overview: A push to main is rejected because a teammate pushed first; integrate their commits with a rebase, resolve if needed, and push again successfully.
codeExamples.code:
# 1) You made a local commit and try to push to main
git push origin main
#    -> REJECTED: the remote has commits you don't have (non-fast-forward)

# 2) Bring the remote's new commits in and replay YOUR commit on top
git pull --rebase origin main
#    (a plain 'git pull' would merge instead and create a merge commit)

# 3) If a conflict stops the rebase, edit the file to resolve, then continue
#    (Git marks conflicts with <<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>> in the file)
git add models/customers.sql
git rebase --continue
#    to bail out entirely instead: git rebase --abort

# 4) Now your commit sits on top of the latest remote main -> push succeeds
git push origin main

# 5) Confirm you are in sync with the remote
git status
codeExamples.breakdown: The first push is rejected because 'origin/main' advanced (a teammate pushed) so your push is not a fast-forward. 'git pull --rebase origin main' fetches their commits and then replays your local commit on top of them, producing a clean linear history without a merge commit. If the same lines were changed, the rebase pauses on a conflict; you edit the file to resolve the '<<<<<<<'/'>>>>>>>' markers, 'git add' the resolved file, and 'git rebase --continue' to finish (or 'git rebase --abort' to undo). With your commit now descending from the latest remote main, the second 'git push' is a fast-forward and is accepted. 'git status' confirms you're up to date. Never fix this with 'git push --force' on a shared branch - it would discard your teammate's commits.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
$ git push origin main
To github.com:team/pipelines.git
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (non-fast-forward)
error: failed to push some refs to 'github.com:team/pipelines.git'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do
hint: not have locally. This is usually caused by another repository pushing
hint: to the same ref. You may want to first integrate the remote changes
hint: (e.g., 'git pull ...') before pushing again.
$ git pull --rebase origin main
From github.com:team/pipelines
 * branch            main       -> FETCH_HEAD
   7a1c9de..b34f0e2  main       -> origin/main
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/main.
$ git push origin main
Enumerating objects: 5, done.
Writing objects: 100% (3/3), 341 bytes | 341.00 KiB/s, done.
To github.com:team/pipelines.git
   b34f0e2..e91a7c4  main -> main
$ git status
On branch main
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.
nothing to commit, working tree clean
codeExamples.commonIssues: Panic-reaching for 'git push --force' after a rejection overwrites the remote and can erase a colleague's commits - almost never correct on shared branches. A rebase can pause on conflicts; forgetting to 'git add' the resolved file before 'git rebase --continue' leaves it stuck. If you truly must rewrite your own branch's history, use '--force-with-lease' (safer than '--force') so you don't clobber unexpected remote changes.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Pull (or fetch) frequently so your local branch rarely diverges far from the remote, minimizing conflicts. Standardize on 'git pull --rebase' team-wide for a clean linear history. On protected branches you can't push to directly anyway - the fix is to open a PR and let GitHub merge, sidestepping manual non-fast-forward pushes entirely.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A three-person analytics-engineering team maintains a shared dbt + Airflow repository that deploys to production. They need to collaborate on it without overwriting each other, ensure every change is reviewed and tested before it reaches production, and keep credentials out of the codebase.
endToEndExample.inputData: A Git repository of pipeline code (Airflow DAGs, dbt models and tests, SQL) hosted on GitHub as 'team/pipelines' with a protected 'main' branch, plus a GitHub Actions workflow that runs 'dbt build' and SQL linting on every push and pull request.
endToEndExample.architecture: GitHub hosts the canonical remote ('origin'); each engineer clones it over SSH. Work happens on short-lived feature branches pushed to origin; changes are proposed via pull requests that trigger GitHub Actions CI. Branch protection on main requires one approving review and a passing CI check before merge, after which a deploy workflow ships the pipeline. Secrets live in GitHub Actions encrypted secrets and a secrets manager, never in the repo (enforced by .gitignore and secret scanning).
processingSteps: 1. Each engineer clones the repo once: 'git clone git@github.com:team/pipelines.git', which downloads full history and configures 'origin' automatically.

2. To start work, an engineer syncs main ('git switch main && git pull') then branches: 'git switch -c feature/add-orders-model', edits the dbt model, commits, and publishes with 'git push -u origin feature/add-orders-model'.
3. They open a pull request into main ('gh pr create --fill'); GitHub Actions automatically runs dbt build and linting against the proposed change and reports pass/fail on the PR.
4. A teammate meanwhile merged a fix to main, so this engineer's later push is rejected as non-fast-forward; they run 'git pull --rebase', resolve a small conflict, and push again cleanly.

5. A reviewer reads the diff, requests a change, the engineer pushes an update (CI re-runs), the reviewer approves, and with a green CI check plus one approval satisfied, the PR merges into the protected main branch.
6. The merge to main triggers the deploy workflow, which ships the updated pipeline; the engineer deletes the feature branch locally and on the remote to keep things tidy.
endToEndExample.output: The orders staging model is live in production, its change is fully recorded on GitHub (commits, the PR discussion, review approval, and CI logs), main was never touched by an untested change, and no secrets were committed.
endToEndExample.monitoring: GitHub shows CI status on every push and PR; branch-protection rules block merges without a passing check and approval; the deploy workflow's status confirms the pipeline shipped, and alerts fire on failed CI or failed deploys.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: A rejected non-fast-forward push is resolved by 'git pull --rebase' and re-pushing; failing CI blocks the merge until the author fixes the code; a conflict during rebase is resolved with 'git add' + 'git rebase --continue'; an accidentally committed secret is caught by secret scanning before merge and the credential is rotated.
endToEndExample.finalResult: A pipeline change moved safely from one engineer's laptop to production through push, pull request, review, and automated testing - demonstrating how remotes, push/pull, and GitHub's collaboration and CI features together let a team change shared pipeline code without breaking main or leaking secrets.

industryUseCases.company: Analytics-engineering teams collaborating on a dbt repository
industryUseCases.problem: Multiple analysts editing the same dbt models risked overwriting each other's work and shipping untested SQL straight to the warehouse.
industryUseCases.solution: Host the dbt project on GitHub with a protected main branch; each analyst branches, pushes, and opens a pull request that triggers GitHub Actions to run 'dbt build' and tests, requiring review and green CI before merge.
industryUseCases.benefits: No untested SQL reaches production, every change is reviewed and traceable, and analysts collaborate on one shared repo without clobbering each other's work.

industryUseCases.company: Data platform teams running Airflow DAGs from Git (GitOps)
industryUseCases.problem: Deploying Airflow DAGs by manually copying files to servers was error-prone, hard to audit, and easy to get out of sync across environments.
industryUseCases.solution: Keep all DAGs in a GitHub repo; engineers push feature branches and open PRs, and a CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions) syncs the merged main branch to the Airflow environment automatically after tests pass.
industryUseCases.benefits: DAG deployments become reviewable, repeatable, and auditable; the repo is the single source of truth, and rollbacks are as easy as reverting a commit.

industryUseCases.problem: External contributors need to propose changes to a project they don't have write access to, without disrupting the maintainers' main repository.
industryUseCases.solution: Contributors fork the repo (their own server-side copy = origin), add the original as 'upstream', push branches to their fork, and open pull requests to the original; maintainers review, run CI, and merge.
industryUseCases.benefits: Anyone can contribute safely without write access, maintainers keep full control of what merges, and 'git fetch upstream' keeps forks current with the source project.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Standardize a branching model (short-lived feature branches, trunk-based development, or GitFlow) and require pull requests so many contributors change one repo safely; choose monorepo vs many repos deliberately, and use shallow clones and fetches rather than full re-clones to keep CI fast as history grows.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Git's distributed design means every clone is a complete backup of history; a remote outage doesn't lose committed work, and pushing important branches regularly ensures nothing critical lives only on a single developer's machine. Mirror the remote to a second host if the repo is business-critical.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Rely on the hosting provider's SLA for the remote, but design so a temporary GitHub outage only blocks merges and CI, not local development - engineers keep committing locally and push when the remote returns. Keep deploy artifacts reproducible from any clone.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Because full history lives in every clone and can be re-pushed, recovery from remote data loss is straightforward; still, keep an automated mirror or backup of the remote, store CI/CD workflow definitions in the repo itself, and document how to re-point 'origin' to a restored or alternate host.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Keep repos lean by excluding large data and binaries (use Git LFS or external object storage, and a strict .gitignore); use '--depth 1' shallow clones and path filters in CI, fetch incrementally instead of re-cloning, and cache dependencies in GitHub Actions to speed pipelines.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Run CI early to catch failures cheaply (a failed test costs seconds; a broken production load costs hours), scope GitHub Actions workflows to relevant paths and cache dependencies to limit billed minutes, and avoid bloating the repo with data that inflates clone and storage costs.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Never commit secrets: enforce .gitignore, enable secret scanning and push protection, store credentials in GitHub Actions encrypted secrets or a secrets manager, prefer SSH keys or short-lived tokens over long-lived passwords (deprecated by GitHub), require 2FA and optionally signed commits, and lock down who can push to or merge into protected branches.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track CI results on pushes and PRs, watch for direct pushes or force-pushes to protected branches, monitor deploy-workflow outcomes triggered by merges to main, and audit the commit and PR history (who changed what, who approved) for compliance.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Gate merges on CI that runs data tests (dbt tests, schema checks, SQL linting) against the proposed change so pipeline changes are validated before reaching main; require these checks in branch protection so they cannot be bypassed.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: GitHub Actions logs record every CI run and deploy; configure notifications and alerts on failed CI, failed deploys after merge, secret-scanning hits, and protected-branch violations so the team is paged before a bad change or leak spreads.

recommendedPractices: **Pull (or fetch) before you start and before you push:** sync with 'git pull --rebase' so your branch rarely diverges far from the remote, minimizing non-fast-forward rejections and conflicts.
**Work on feature branches and merge via pull requests:** never commit directly to a shared main; open a PR so changes are reviewed and CI-tested before merging.
**Set the upstream on first push:** always use 'git push -u origin <branch>' so later syncs are just 'git push'/'git pull' and 'git status' reports ahead/behind.
**Protect the main branch:** require at least one review and a passing CI check before merge so no untested pipeline change reaches production.
**Keep secrets and large data out of the repo:** use .gitignore, secret scanning, a secrets manager, and external storage / Git LFS for big files.
engineeringStandards: Prefer SSH keys or short-lived tokens for authentication over long-lived passwords (GitHub deprecated password auth for Git operations in 2021).
Never use 'git push --force' on shared branches; if you must rewrite your own branch's history, use '--force-with-lease' and only after coordinating.
Resolve a rejected non-fast-forward push by integrating first ('git pull --rebase'), then pushing - not by forcing.
designRecommendations: Choose and document one workflow (shared-repo + PR for internal teams, fork + PR for open source) and one pull strategy (merge vs rebase) so the team is consistent.
Keep feature branches short-lived and focused on one change so PRs are small, reviewable, and quick to merge.
Store CI/CD and deployment definitions (GitHub Actions workflows) in the repo so the pipeline is versioned and reproducible from any clone.
namingConventions: Name feature branches descriptively with a type prefix, e.g. 'feature/add-orders-model' or 'fix/customers-null-key'.
Keep the primary branch named 'main' and the default remote named 'origin' (and 'upstream' for a fork's source) to match universal conventions.
Write clear, imperative commit messages ('Add orders staging model') that read well in the remote history and PR list.
documentationStandards: Include a README explaining how to clone the repo, set up authentication, and run the pipeline locally.
Document the branching and PR workflow, required reviews, and CI checks so new contributors know the process.
Provide a CONTRIBUTING guide (especially for forked/open-source projects) covering how to add 'upstream', keep a fork in sync, and open a PR.
testingStrategies: Run automated tests and linting in GitHub Actions on every push and pull request so failures are caught before merge.
Make CI checks required in branch protection so a PR cannot merge into main unless tests pass.
Test the collaboration flow itself: verify a rejected push is resolved via pull --rebase and re-push, and that a PR from a feature branch merges cleanly after review.

commonMistakes.mistake: Force-pushing to a shared branch after a rejected (non-fast-forward) push.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The rejection message is confusing and 'git push --force' makes it 'go away' instantly, so beginners reach for it without understanding it overwrites remote history.
commonMistakes.impact: It discards the commits a teammate pushed while you were working, losing their work and corrupting the shared branch's history - a hard, sometimes unrecoverable problem on a busy repo.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Integrate first: 'git pull --rebase' (or 'git pull') to bring in the remote commits and replay yours on top, resolve any conflicts, then push - now a clean fast-forward. Reserve '--force-with-lease' for rewriting your own branch history only.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming 'git push' backs up all your work, when it only uploads pushed branches.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: People treat GitHub like automatic cloud sync (like Dropbox) rather than an explicit push of specific committed branches.
commonMistakes.impact: Un-pushed branches and uncommitted changes exist only on the laptop; a lost or wiped machine loses that work entirely, sometimes days of it.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Commit early and push branches regularly with 'git push -u origin <branch>'; treat only what's on the remote as safe, and never leave important work un-pushed for long.

commonMistakes.mistake: Committing and pushing secrets (API keys, passwords, connection strings) to the repo.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Credentials get hard-coded during quick local testing and then swept up by 'git add .' and pushed without noticing.
commonMistakes.impact: The secret is now in the shared remote's history (and every clone) and must be treated as compromised; removing it from history is painful and the credential must be rotated.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Keep secrets in environment variables / a secrets manager, add them to .gitignore, use GitHub Actions encrypted secrets, and enable secret scanning with push protection so leaks are blocked before they reach the remote.

comparisonSection.explanation: Fetch downloads new remote commits into your remote-tracking branches (like origin/main) and stops there - your working files and current branch are untouched, so it's always safe and lets you inspect changes with 'git log main..origin/main' before integrating. Pull runs that same fetch and then merges (or rebases with --rebase) the changes into your current branch, which is where merge commits and conflicts can appear. Use fetch to look before you leap; use pull to actually bring the remote's work into your branch.

SSH uses a public/private key pair - you register the public key on GitHub and your private key stays local, so pushes and pulls need no password prompts once set up; great for daily development. HTTPS uses your username plus a Personal Access Token (plain account passwords were deprecated by GitHub in 2021), which is easy through firewalls and simple to start with but requires managing/rotating tokens (often cached by a credential helper). Both are secure; SSH is smoother for regular use, HTTPS is more universally reachable.

In the shared-repo model - typical for internal data teams - everyone has write access to one repository, creates feature branches, pushes to 'origin', and opens PRs into a protected main; it's simple because there's one shared remote. In the fork model - typical for open source and contributors without write access - you fork to your own server-side copy (origin), add the original as 'upstream', push to your fork, and open a PR to the original repo. Both converge on 'branch, propose via PR, review + CI, merge'; the difference is whether you push to the shared repo or your own fork.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is a Git remote, and what is 'origin'?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A remote is a named reference in your repository's config that points to the URL of another copy of the same repo, usually one hosted on a platform like GitHub. 'origin' is the conventional default name Git gives the remote you cloned from (or the first one you add). You inspect remotes with 'git remote -v' and add one with 'git remote add origin <url>'. Push, fetch, and pull all target a remote by this name.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: The interviewer wants the core mental model: a remote is just a nickname for a URL of a shared copy, and 'origin' is the default nickname. Mentioning 'git remote -v' and 'git remote add' shows hands-on familiarity.

beginnerQuestions.question: What's the difference between Git and GitHub?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Git is the open-source version-control tool that runs locally and tracks your project's history - it works with no internet and no account. GitHub is a hosting-and-collaboration platform built on top of Git: it stores the remote copy and adds features Git itself doesn't have, like pull requests, code review, issues, forks, and GitHub Actions for CI/CD. You can use Git without GitHub, and Git can push to other hosts like GitLab or Bitbucket too.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: This tests whether the candidate conflates the tool with the platform. The strong answer separates 'Git manages history locally' from 'GitHub hosts the remote and adds collaboration', and notes Git works with other hosts.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between 'git fetch' and 'git pull'?
intermediateQuestions.answer: 'git fetch' downloads new commits from the remote into your remote-tracking branches (like origin/main) but does not change your working files or current branch, so it's always safe and lets you inspect what changed first. 'git pull' does that same fetch and then immediately merges (or rebases, with --rebase) those commits into your current branch, which is where merge commits and conflicts can occur. In short, fetch is 'download only', pull is 'download and integrate'.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: The key insight is that pull adds the merge/rebase step. Mentioning that fetch is safe and lets you preview with 'git log main..origin/main' shows practical understanding of when to use each.

intermediateQuestions.question: You try to push and get 'Updates were rejected... non-fast-forward'. What happened and how do you fix it?
intermediateQuestions.answer: The remote branch has commits you don't have locally - usually a teammate pushed while you were working - so moving the remote pointer to your commit would discard theirs, and the server rejects the push. The correct fix is to integrate first: 'git pull --rebase' (or 'git pull') to download their commits and replay yours on top, resolve any conflicts, then push again as a clean fast-forward. You should not use 'git push --force' on a shared branch because it would overwrite their work.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want you to name the cause (remote has commits you lack), give the safe fix (pull/rebase then push), and explicitly reject force-pushing on shared branches - a common dangerous mistake.

advancedQuestions.question: How would you set up a data team to collaborate on a shared pipeline repo so main is always deployable?
advancedQuestions.answer: Host the repo on GitHub with a protected main branch. Engineers clone once, then for each change sync main, create a short-lived feature branch, push it with 'git push -u origin <branch>', and open a pull request. Branch protection requires at least one approving review and a passing GitHub Actions CI check (tests, linting, dbt build) before merge, so no untested change reaches main; a merge to main triggers the deploy workflow. Keep secrets out of the repo via .gitignore, secret scanning, and encrypted Actions secrets.
advancedQuestions.explanation: This tests production maturity: feature branches + PRs, required review and CI, branch protection, CI/CD on merge, and secret management. Bonus for mentioning short-lived branches and a consistent pull (rebase) strategy.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain the fork-and-pull-request workflow and how you keep a fork up to date.
advancedQuestions.answer: For a project you can't push to directly (open source), you fork it - GitHub makes your own server-side copy, which you clone as 'origin'. You add the original repo as a second remote, 'upstream'. You push feature branches to your fork and open a pull request from your fork's branch to the original repo, where maintainers review and merge. To keep your fork current, you 'git fetch upstream' and merge or rebase 'upstream/main' into your local main, then push it to your fork. This is how contributors participate without write access while maintainers keep control of what merges.
advancedQuestions.explanation: The interviewer checks understanding of multiple remotes (origin = your fork, upstream = source), cross-repo PRs, and syncing a fork. Tie it to real open-source data tooling contributions.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A junior engineer's push to the shared 'main' branch keeps failing with a non-fast-forward error, and in frustration they're about to run 'git push --force'. You catch it in time. What do you tell them to do, and why not force?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: The rejection means the remote main advanced with commits they don't have - someone else pushed. Force-pushing would move remote main to their commit and drop the other commits, losing a teammate's work and rewriting shared history. The safe path is to integrate the remote's commits first, then push as a normal fast-forward. Rebase keeps history linear; merge also works. Also note that on a properly protected main they shouldn't be pushing directly at all - they should use a PR.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Explain that the remote has commits they're missing, so 'git push --force' would erase a teammate's work - never do that on a shared branch. Instead run 'git pull --rebase' (or 'git pull') to download the remote commits and replay their commit on top, resolve any conflicts with 'git add' + 'git rebase --continue', then push again, which now succeeds as a fast-forward. Longer term, protect main and require changes to go through pull requests so nobody pushes directly, and pull frequently to avoid large divergence. If they ever must rewrite only their own branch, use '--force-with-lease', not '--force'.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design the Git/GitHub workflow and CI/CD for a data engineering team that develops Airflow DAGs and dbt models and must ship them safely to production many times a day.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Host one shared repo on GitHub with a protected main branch. Developers clone over SSH, work on short-lived feature branches, push with '-u', and open pull requests. GitHub Actions runs tests, linting, and 'dbt build' on every push and PR; branch protection requires a passing CI check plus at least one review before merge. A merge to main triggers a deploy workflow that syncs DAGs/models to the target environment. Secrets live in encrypted Actions secrets and a secrets manager, enforced by .gitignore, secret scanning, and push protection.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Requiring reviews and CI slows down each merge but prevents untested changes reaching production; a shared-repo model is simpler than forks but needs disciplined branch protection. Rebase pulls give clean history but require comfort with conflict resolution; merge is simpler but noisier. GitHub-specific automation speeds delivery but adds platform dependence, and a GitHub outage can block merges/CI (though local Git work continues).
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: As the team grows, keep branches short-lived (trunk-based), split into multiple repos or a well-structured monorepo, use shallow clones and path-filtered/cached CI to keep pipelines fast, add required status checks and code-owner reviews per area, and mirror the remote for disaster recovery. Rely on Git's distributed nature so every clone is a full backup and any developer can re-push after a remote incident.

followUpQuestions: What does 'git push -u origin main' do, and why does the '-u' flag matter for later pushes and pulls?
When would you choose SSH over HTTPS for a remote, and what changed about GitHub password authentication in 2021?
What is the difference between 'git pull' and 'git pull --rebase', and why might a team standardize on rebase?
How do 'origin' and 'upstream' differ in a forked-repository workflow, and how do you keep the fork in sync?
How does branch protection combined with GitHub Actions keep an untested change from reaching production?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: A remote (default 'origin') is a named reference to a hosted copy of your repo; push uploads local commits, fetch downloads remote commits without merging, pull does fetch + merge, and GitHub is the platform that hosts the remote and adds pull requests, review, and CI/CD on top of Git.
keyConcepts: A remote is a nickname for a URL of another copy of the repo; 'origin' is the default, set automatically by 'git clone' or manually via 'git remote add'.
Push uploads your commits; fetch downloads remote commits into origin/main without touching your files; pull = fetch + merge (or rebase) into your current branch.
'git push -u origin <branch>' sets the upstream so later 'git push'/'git pull' need no arguments and 'git status' shows ahead/behind.
A non-fast-forward rejection means the remote has commits you lack - pull/rebase first, then push; never force-push a shared branch.
Git is the local tool; GitHub is the hosting platform that adds pull requests, code review, issues, forks, protected branches, and Actions CI/CD.
commands: git clone git@github.com:team/pipelines.git        # copy a repo and set 'origin' automatically
git remote add origin git@github.com:team/pipelines.git   # connect a local repo to a remote
git push -u origin main            # publish main and set it as the upstream branch
git fetch origin                   # download remote commits (safe, no merge)
git pull --rebase                  # fetch + replay your commits on top (fix a non-fast-forward)
gh pr create --fill                # open a GitHub pull request from the current branch
interviewPoints: A remote is a named URL; 'origin' is the default, and clone sets it up for you.
Fetch = download only (safe); pull = fetch + merge/rebase into your branch.
A non-fast-forward rejection means the remote moved - pull/rebase first, don't force-push.
Git manages history locally; GitHub hosts the remote and adds PRs, review, and CI/CD.
Use branches + pull requests + protected main + CI so no untested change reaches production.
quickNotes: 'git push' only uploads pushed branches - un-pushed/uncommitted work is NOT backed up.
HTTPS needs a Personal Access Token (passwords deprecated by GitHub in 2021); SSH uses a key pair.
'git branch -vv' shows each local branch's upstream; 'git status' reports ahead/behind of it.
'--force-with-lease' is the safer force; never plain '--force' on a shared branch.
Fork workflow: origin = your fork, upstream = the original; 'git fetch upstream' to stay current.

keyTakeaways: A remote is a named reference (default 'origin') to a hosted copy of your repository; 'git clone' sets origin up automatically, 'git remote add origin <url>' connects an existing local repo, and 'git push -u origin <branch>' publishes a branch and sets its upstream so future syncs are one word.

Push uploads your local commits to the remote, fetch downloads the remote's commits into remote-tracking branches without changing your files (always safe), and pull is fetch plus a merge or rebase into your current branch - so fetch is 'show me' and pull is 'show me and combine it in'.

A push is rejected as non-fast-forward when the remote has commits you don't have; the correct fix is to integrate first with 'git pull --rebase' (or pull) and push again - never 'git push --force' on a shared branch, which would erase teammates' work.

Git is the local version-control tool while GitHub is a hosting-and-collaboration platform built on it, adding pull requests, code review, issues, forks, protected branches, and GitHub Actions CI/CD - the foundation of how data teams review and test pipeline code before it reaches production.

In practice, data teams collaborate via short-lived feature branches and pull requests into a protected main branch, with CI running tests and linting on every push, secrets kept out of the repo, and either a shared-repo flow (internal teams) or a fork-and-PR flow (open source).
